questions.qtext:
Which of the following(s) function declarations can be used to pass the following array?

char myArray[3][4];
questions.solution:
Answer: B, C, A

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

Answer: B, C

int a [5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; While passing this into a function we don’t really care about the size (although we should and that must be passsed as another integer argument). a is an array of intergers so we use a pointer to an integer to work with it.

Similarly char myArray[3][4] is an array of 3 “objects/rows” where each object/row itself is an array of 4 chars.

a b c d
e f g h
i j k l

So to work in this situation we need a pointer that points to an array of four charcters: char (*ptr)[4].

Now void fun(char ptr[X][4]); is internally translated to char (*ptr)[4] only and ‘X’ can be any value, that will be ignored by the compiler.

A: Wrong, missing the crucial details, the size of row.

D: Note this: Double pointers has nothing to do with 2D arrays, they are not related in any manner.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)
function declarationvalid? reason
void fun(char a[3][]);invalidWhen passing 2D array, only the first dimension can be omitted, not the second. Here 2nd dimension is missing so compiler doesn’t know the size of each row → invalid.
void fun(char a[][4]);validHere the 2nd dimension (4) is known, so compiler can calculate row-to-row jump. First dimension is optional while passing array → so this works.
void fun(char (*a)[4]);validThis is the exact decay type. myArray decays to pointer to an array of 4 chars (char (*)[4]). So this matches the true type → valid.
void fun(char **a);invalidchar** means pointer to pointer to char, which is a completely different type. 2D array pointer is NOT equal to pointer-to-pointer → so not acceptable.
Source solution 3 (score: 1)

In C, when you pass a 2D array (like $\texttt{char\ myArray[3][4]}$) to a function, it "decays" into a pointer to its first element. The first element of a 2D array is a 1D array (a row). Therefore, the array decays into a pointer to an array of $4$ characters.

To access an element like $\texttt{a[i][j]}$, the compiler needs to calculate its exact memory address using this formula:

$$\text{Address} = \text{Base\_Address} + (i \times \text{number\_of\_columns} + j) \times \text{size\_of\_type}$$

Because $\text{number_of_columns}$ is required for this calculation, the compiler must know the inner dimension(s) of the array. The first dimension (number of rows) is not needed for this calculation, which is why it can be left blank.

  • A. $\texttt{void\ fun(char\ a[3][]);}$
    Incorrect. The compiler needs to know the size of the columns to perform pointer arithmetic. Leaving the second set of brackets empty is illegal in C.
  • B. $\texttt{void\ fun(char\ a[][4]);}$
    Correct. The first dimension can be omitted when declaring a function parameter, but the second dimension, $4$, is explicitly provided. This gives the compiler the information it needs.
  • C. $\texttt{void\ fun(char\ (*a)[4]);}$
    Correct. This is exactly what $\texttt{myArray}$ decays into. It declares $\texttt{a}$ as a pointer to an array of $4$ characters. In the context of function parameters, option B and option C are completely equivalent to the compiler.
  • D. $\texttt{void\ fun(char\ **a);}$
    Incorrect. $\texttt{char\ **a}$ is a pointer to a pointer, often used to point to an array of string literals or dynamically allocated row pointers. A standard 2D array like $\texttt{char\ myArray[3][4]}$ is a single, contiguous block of memory. It does not decay into a double pointer, so passing it to this function would result in incompatible pointer type errors.

questions.qtext:
What will be printed by the following program?

#include<stdio.h> 
struct card
{
 int face ;
};
typedef struct card Card ;
Card c ;
void pass(Card c);
int main()
{
 c.face = 1;
 printf("%d ", c.face);
 pass(c);
 printf("%d",c.face);
}
void pass(Card c)
{
 c.face = 5;
 printf("%d ",c.face);
}
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

Answer: B

1. #include<stdio.h> 
2. int c;
3. void pass(int x);
4. int main()
5. {
6. c = 1;
7. printf("%d ", c);
8. pass(c);
9. printf("%d", c);
10. }
11. 
12. void pass(int x)
13. {
14. x = 5;
15. printf("%d ",x);
16. }

I just changed the user defined datatype “Card” to int for easy to understand line-by-line analysis.

line 2: ‘c’ is a global integer variable with default initial value 0. Similarly line 7 in question, ‘c’ is a global ‘Card’ variable with default int member (face) initial value 0.

line 6: ‘c’ is not declared in this scope so the ‘c’ from outer (global) scope is used since C (the language) has static scoping. Similarly line 11 in question.

line 7: value of global ‘c’ is printed: 1.

line 8: value of ‘c’ is passed into the function, not the address of ‘c’. Similarly line 13 in question

The general misconception around structures is that just as in array “int a[2] = {1, 2};” ‘a’ is the alias for memory location, and when it (a) is passed in the function the changes are persistent, same must happen with structures also. But this is not the case, using structure we define a “type”. it may look like an array as it has various data inside of it (‘face’ in this case) but it is not.

Coming back to pass(), a quick way to avoid confusion is to rename all the local variables, now you see ‘x’ is local to pass() and anything that happens to it here, remains here.

line 9: ‘c’ still is 1.

Source solution 2 (score: 3)

Global Declaration $:$
$\texttt{Card\ c;}$ declares a global variable named $\texttt{c}$ of type $\texttt{Card}$.

Inside $\texttt{main()}:$

  • $\texttt{c.face\ =\ 1;}$: The global variable $\texttt{c}$ is updated so its $\texttt{face}$ value is $1$.

  • $\texttt{printf("\%d\ ",\ c.face);}$: This prints the current value of the global $\texttt{c.face}$, outputting our first number: $\texttt{1\ }$.

Function Call - $\texttt{pass(c);}:$

  • The program calls the $\texttt{pass}$ function and passes the global variable $\texttt{c}$ to it.

  • Crucial Concept (Pass by Value): In C, when you pass a $\texttt{struct}$ to a function, it is passed by value. This means a complete, independent copy of the struct is created for the function to use.

Inside $\texttt{pass(Card\ c)}:$

  • The parameter here is also named $\texttt{c}$. Because it is a local parameter, it shadows (hides) the global variable $\texttt{c}$ for the duration of this function.

  • $\texttt{c.face\ =\ 5;}$: This updates the local copy's $\texttt{face}$ value to $5$. The global variable back in $\texttt{main}$ is completely untouched and remains $1$.

  • $\texttt{printf("\%d\ ",\ c.face);}$: This prints the local copy's value, outputting the second number: $\texttt{5\ }$.

Back in $\texttt{main()}:$

  • $\texttt{printf("\%d",\ c.face);}$: The function returns, and the local copy from $\texttt{pass}$ is destroyed. We are back to looking at the global variable $\texttt{c}$. Since it was never changed by the function, its $\texttt{face}$ is still $1$. It outputs the final number: $\texttt{1}$.

Final Output: $\texttt{1\ 5\ 1}$

questions.qtext:
Consider below two files p$1$.c and p$2$.c

We compile both files independently and link them in case the compilation is successful.

Which of the following(s) is/are TRUE?

options.text: p$1$.c can not be compiled as there is no main function in the file.
Line $3$ in p$1$.c will produce a compilation error because of the redefinition of variable $a.$
Line $6$ in p$2$.c will produce a compilation error since the extern does not allocate memory to variables.
Line $7$ in p$2$.c will produce a compilation error.

questions.solution:
Answer: D, A

Source solution 1 (score: 22)

Answer: D

A: This is clearly wrong, main() is what called by the O.S. when the program executes. The program without main() can be compiled without any issues, however problem may arise during the linking step (more in comments below).

B: This is also wrong because the so called “redefinition” is inside curly braces (block). So this in fact is not redefinition.

C: Extern by definition does not allocate memory, using extern only declares the variables, not define (allocate memory) them. As far as compilation is concerned this will compile without any issue. This however will not be linked because the definition of ‘b’ in p1.c is of type static and static variables are not available to the linker.

D: variable ‘a’ is used before it is defined. C (language) has static scoping so it looks for variable ‘a’ in global scope of p2.c and there also ‘a’ is not found. This would be correct if “extern int a;” was typed before using it.

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

A. $\texttt{p1.c}$ can not be compiled as there is no $\texttt{main}$ function in the file.

  • False. In C, a source file does not need a $\texttt{main()}$ function to be compiled. It can be compiled independently into an object file (e.g., using $\texttt{gcc\ -c\ p1.c}$). The $\texttt{main()}$ function is only required during the linking phase to create a final executable program.


B. Line $3$ in $\texttt{p1.c}$ will produce a compilation error because of the redefinition of variable $\texttt{a}$.

  • False. This is a concept known as variable shadowing.
    void f2(int a) { // 'a' is a parameter
 {
 int a; // (3) New block scope begins
 a = 1;
 }
}
    In C, when you declare a variable inside a new block $\texttt{\{\ ...\ \}}$, it is perfectly legal for it to have the same name as a variable in an outer scope (like the function parameter $\texttt{a}$). The inner $\texttt{a}$ simply "shadows" or hides the outer $\texttt{a}$ for the duration of that block. It will not cause a compilation error.

C. Line $6$ in $\texttt{p2.c}$ will produce a compilation error since the $\texttt{extern}$ does not allocate memory to variables.

  • False. The declaration $\texttt{extern\ int\ b;}$ is valid. It tells the compiler that $\texttt{b}$ is defined somewhere else.
    void f5() {
 extern int b;
 b = 1; // (6)
}
    The compiler will successfully compile this code without error. If the variable $\texttt{b}$ cannot be found later when the files are stitched together, it will result in a linker error, not a compilation error. (Note: Because $\texttt{b}$ is declared as $\texttt{static\ int\ b;}$ in $\texttt{p1.c}$, its scope is restricted to $\texttt{p1.c}$ only, so this will indeed cause a linker error later, but the compilation of $\texttt{p2.c}$ itself succeeds).

D. Line $7$ in $\texttt{p2.c}$ will produce a compilation error.

  • True. Look at the $\texttt{main()}$ function in $\texttt{p2.c}$:
    int main() {
 a = 1; // (7)
 // ...
}
    For this to be valid, $\texttt{a}$ must be declared somewhere visible to $\texttt{main()}$. There is no global variable $\texttt{a}$ in $\texttt{p2.c}$. While there is an $\texttt{extern\ int\ a;}$ declaration inside $\texttt{f4()}$, that declaration is local to the scope of $\texttt{f4()}$ and is invisible to $\texttt{main()}$. Therefore, when the compiler reaches line $7$, it sees an undeclared identifier $\texttt{a}$ and throws a compilation error.
Source solution 3 (score: 0)
Options AnalysisA) WRONG

A C file does not necessarily require a main() function. It may be linked with another file that contains main().

Also read this comment

B) WRONG

We are not redefining a. Instead, a new local a is defined inside the block, and it is accessible only within that block.

C) WRONG

Line 6 will create a linker error.
From the compiler's perspective, everything is fine, but the linker cannot resolve b because it is declared as static.

D) CORRECT

Line 7 will indeed produce a compiler error because the compiler does not know that a is extern.

The information that a is extern remains local to f4() and is not visible outside that scope..

Assume that an int variable takes $4$ bytes and a char variable takes $1$ byte. What is the output of the code below?

int main()
{
 int arr[]={10,20,30,40,50,60};
 int *ptr1=arr;
 int *ptr2=arr+5;
 printf("Number of elements between two pointer are: %d.", 
 (ptr2 - ptr1));
 printf("Number of bytes between two pointer are: %d.", 
 (char*)ptr2 - (char*)ptr1);
}

options.text: Number of elements between two pointer are: $5$. Number of bytes between two pointers are: $20$
Number of elements between two pointer are: $20.$ Number of bytes between two pointers are: $20$
Number of elements between two pointer are: $5.$ Number of bytes between two pointers are: $5$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

Let Assume Starting Address is 1000

then adress of arr[0] is 1000=ptr1 and adress of arr[5] =1000+(5*4)=1020=ptr2

now, ptr2-ptr1= (1020-1000)/size of(*ptr1)=5

(char*)ptr2 – (char*)ptr1=(1020-1000)/size of(*ptr1)=20[such that here p1 and p2 both is typecasted).

So The answer is option A.

Source solution 2 (score: 7)

Answer: A

Question basically asks the number of objects/cells/elements of “type” between two pointers.

ptr1 and ptr2 are pointer of type int. ptr1 = arr + 0, and ptr2 = arr + 5. This one is straight-forward 5.

Now the char typecasted pointers have how many elements of type char? It has 5 ints and sizeof one int is 4 * size of one char, so total 20 char elements.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

$\texttt{ptr1}$ points to $\texttt{arr[0]}$ and $\texttt{ptr2}$ points to $\texttt{arr[5]}$.

For $\texttt{int *}$ pointer subtraction, the difference is counted in number of elements, so $\texttt{ptr2 - ptr1 = 5}$.

After casting to $\texttt{char *}$, the difference is counted in bytes.

Since one $\texttt{int}$ takes $4$ bytes, the byte difference is $5 \times 4 = 20$.

So the output is:

$\texttt{Number of elements between two pointer are: 5. Number of bytes between two pointer are: 20.}$

Correct option: A

questions.qtext:
What is the output of the following code?

#include<stdio.h>
int main() {
 unsigned int x = 1;
 int y = -2;
 (x + y > 0) ? printf("WRONG ANSWER") : printf("CORRECT ANSWER");
}
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 10)

x = 1 = 000...001 (bit pattern of 1)

y = – 2 = 111...110 (bit pattern of – 2)

x + y = – 1 = 111...111 (bit patten of – 1), since x is unsigned int and y is signed int, so y will be promoted to unsigned int, resultant x + y will also be unsigned int.

(x+y > 0) = ( 111...111 > 000...000 ) = True, x+y is unsigned int, since it is comparison between 2 unsigned numbers. (2^32 – 1 > 0)

Thus, program will print “Wrong Answer”.

Answer – A

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

-1 in Unsigned representation is all 1's i.e Max Unsigned Number.

Now, -2 is equal to (Max Unsigned Number - 1)

So, generally speaking let any negative integer -k :

When type casted to unsigned int it becomes : [Max Unsigned - (k-1)]

Finally we can say : ( x + y ) becomes : Max Unsigned - (1) + 1 i.e 11111..111 all 1’s & evaluates to True

Therefore, o/p is “WRONG ANSWER”

void mystery(int n) {
 if (n <= 1) {
 printf("%d", n);
 }
 else {
 printf("%d, ", n);
 mystery(n/2);
 printf(", %d", n);
 }
}

What will be the output printed by $\text{mystery(12)}?$
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

Explained using Tree Method it helps in visualization.

  1. The statements written in black ink are executed at call time i.e executed before the next recursive call.

  2. The statements written in red ink are executed while returning i.e “basically the value of n is saved in activation record of the function call and executed while returning”

Here, if you observe the statements in red they are returning the value stored in the previous function call.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Answer: A

First line 1 will be executed then another function call is made now when that function will return then line 3 will be executed.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

The function $\texttt{mystery(n)}$ uses recursion. When $\texttt{n}$ is greater than $1$, it prints the number, calls itself with $\texttt{n/2}$ (integer division), and then prints the number again after the recursive call finishes.

Here is how the call stack builds up and unwinds for $\texttt{mystery(12)}$:

  1. $\texttt{mystery(12)}$ is called:

    • $\texttt{12\ <=\ 1}$ is False.

    • Prints: $\texttt{12,}$

    • Calls $\texttt{mystery(6)}$

    • (Pending action: print $\texttt{, 12}$)

  2. $\texttt{mystery(6)}$ is called:

    • $\texttt{6\ <=\ 1}$ is False.

    • Prints: $\texttt{6,}$

    • Calls $\texttt{mystery(3)}$

    • (Pending action: print $\texttt{,\ 6}$)

  3. $\texttt{mystery(3)}$ is called:

    • $\texttt{3\ <=\ 1}$ is False.

    • Prints: $\texttt{3,}$

    • Calls $\texttt{mystery(1)}$ (Note: $3/2 = 1$ in integer division)

    • (Pending action: print $\texttt{,\ 3}$)

  4. $\texttt{mystery(1)}$ is called:

    • $\texttt{1\ <=\ 1}$ is True.

    • Prints: $\texttt{1}$

    • Function returns.

Unwinding the Stack:

Now, the program goes back to finish the pending actions in reverse order:

  1. Back in $\texttt{mystery(3)}$: Executes its pending action and prints $\texttt{,\ 3}$

  2. Back in $\texttt{mystery(6)}$: Executes its pending action and prints $\texttt{,\ 6}$

  3. Back in $\texttt{mystery(12)}$: Executes its pending action and prints $\texttt{,\ 12}$

Final Output $:\texttt{12,\ 6,\ 3,\ 1,\ 3,\ 6,\ 12}$

What will be the output of the following program?

main()
{
 int a[2][2] = { {1,2},{3,4} };
 int(*p)[2][2];
 p = &a;
 printf("%d", (*p)[0][0]);
}
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 20)

a is an int array of size 2x2.

p is a pointer to int array of size 2x2.

p = &a → p points to array a. Thus, a and *p are now equivalent.

(*p)[0][0] ≣ a[0][0]

Answer :- A

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

p is a pointer to a 2D matrix (‘a’)

doing (*p)[0][0] is equal to doing a[0][0] which results in ‘1’

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

$\texttt{a}$ is a 2D integer array:

$\texttt{int\ a[2][2]\ =\ \{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\};}$

So the array elements are:

$\texttt{a[0][0]\ =\ 1}$,

$\texttt{a[0][1]\ =\ 2}$,

$\texttt{a[1][0]\ =\ 3}$,

$\texttt{a[1][1]\ =\ 4}$.

The declaration

$\texttt{int\ (*p)[2][2];}$

means $\texttt{p}$ is a pointer to a 2D array of size $2 \times 2$.

Notice the parentheses around $\texttt{*p}:$ this forces $\texttt{p}$ to be a pointer to the whole array, rather than an array of pointers.

Then,

$\texttt{p\ = \&a;}$

stores the address of the whole array $\texttt{a}$ in $\texttt{p}$.

Now, $\texttt{p}$ points directly to the 2D array $\texttt{a}$.

Now,

$\texttt{(*p)[0][0]}$

means first dereference $\texttt{p}$ to get the array $\texttt{a}$, then access $\texttt{a[0][0]}$.

Since $\texttt{a[0][0]\ =\ 1}$, the output is: $\texttt{1}$

Correct answer: A

Consider the following declaration of $a$.

int a[100][200][30];

What will be the integer value of $a[50][300] - a[10][500]?$
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 35)

1) Solving by counting no of elements between both pointers (addresses) -

int a[100][200][30];

a[50][300] – a[10][500] = (50 * 200 * 30 + 300 * 30) – (10 * 200 * 30 + 500 * 30) = 234000.

2) Solving by rules of pointer arithmetic -

Let b be the base address of a.

a[50][300] – a[10][500] = [ ( b + (50 * 200 * 30 + 300 * 30) * 4 ) – ( b + (10 * 200 * 30 + 500 * 30) * 4 ) ] / 4 = 234000.

Answer :- 234000.

To understand this 1st you need to understand how to calculate address of 3d array, given 3d array is a[100][200][30] - it means 100 arrays have there own 2d arrays of sizees a[200][30], which have there own 1d array of size a[30]...
The address in c are kept in row major format, okay,
So to know the address of any element in 3d array , for example a[10][100][20],

address of a[10][100][20] is the simply 10 x 200 x 30 (as each of these 10 arrays have 2d arrays [200][30] ) + 100 x 30 (as each of these 100 arrays have there own 30 sized array) + 20 (individual 20 elements address)

So address of a[10][100][20] = (10 x 200 x 30) + (100 x 30 + 20).

Now coming on to question - we need to find the difference of a[50][300] - a[10][500] ??
Difference between the arrays tells us the number of elements between them, and also the third dimension is not mentioned the question so we will assume it is talking about the 1st element of the array so the actual question is a[50][300[0] - a[10][500][0] ?

so difference = a[50][300][0] - a[10][500][0]
☝ ☝
x - y
x = 50 x 200 x 30 (same logic as before ) + 300 x 30 + 0 = 3,00,000 + 9,000 = 309,000
y = (10 x 200 x 30) + (500 x 30) + 0 = 60,000 + 15,000 = 75,000

So, finally x - y = 309,000 - 75,000 = 234,000. (which denotes the number of elements between them)
Source solution 4 (score: 0)

The declaration is $\texttt{int\ a[100][200][30];}$. This means $\texttt{a}$ is a 3D array.

  • $\texttt{a[i]}$ represents a 2D array of size $\texttt{[200][30]}$.

  • $\texttt{a[i][j]}$ represents a 1D array of $30$ integers, that is $\texttt{int[30]}$.


In C, when an array is used in an expression like subtraction, it "decays" into a pointer to its first element. Therefore, both $\texttt{a[50][300]}$ and $\texttt{a[10][500]}$ decay from type $\texttt{int[30]}$ to type $\texttt{int*}$, which is a pointer to an integer.

When you subtract two $\texttt{int*}$ pointers, the compiler calculates the memory distance between them and divides it by $\texttt{sizeof(int)}$. This means the result is simply the difference in the number of integer elements between the two addresses.

Now, we'll calculate the Offsets

Although the indices $300$ and $500$ exceed the declared bound of $200$, C pointer arithmetic treats the multi-dimensional array as a flat, contiguous block of memory. It simply calculates the total offset from the base address.

The formula to find the offset of $\texttt{a[i][j]}$ in terms of the number of integers from the base address is:

$$\text{Offset} = i \times (\text{Elements per 2D block}) + j \times (\text{Elements per 1D row})$$

$$\text{Offset} = i \times (200 \times 30) + j \times (30)$$

Applying the Formula :

  • For $\texttt{a[50][300]}$:

    $\text{Offset}_1 = 50 \times (200 \times 30) + 300 \times 30$

    $\text{Offset}_1 = 50 \times 6000 + 9000$

    $\text{Offset}_1 = 300000 + 9000 = 309000$

  • For $\texttt{a[10][500]}$:

    $\text{Offset}_2 = 10 \times (200 \times 30) + 500 \times 30$

    $\text{Offset}_2 = 10 \times 6000 + 15000$

    $\text{Offset}_2 = 60000 + 15000 = 75000$


Now, we subtract the two offsets to find the number of integers between the two pointers:

$\text{Result} = 309000 - 75000 = 234000$

Final answer: $\boxed{\mathbf{234000}}$

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_point#Sequence_points_in_C_and_C++

Before a function is entered in a function call. The order in which the arguments are evaluated is not specified, but this sequence point means that all of their side effects are complete before the function is entered. In the expression f(i++) + g(j++) + h(k++), f is called with a parameter of the original value of i, but i is incremented before entering the body of f. Similarly, j and k are updated before entering g and h respectively. However, it is not specified in which order f(), g(), h() are executed, nor in which order i, j, k are incremented. If the body of f accesses the variables j and k, it might find both, neither, or just one of them to have been incremented. (The function call f(a,b,c) is not a use of the comma operator; the order of evaluation for a, b, and c is unspecified.)

Correct Answer: A,B,C.

Analysis: The code is:

C

int (*a)[3]; // Pointer to an array of 3 integers
int arr[2][3]; // 2D array
a = arr + 1; // 'a' points to the second row (arr[1])

We need to find the expression equivalent to &arr[1][2].

  1. Understanding a:

    • arr decays to a pointer to its first row.

    • arr + 1 points to the second row (arr[1]).

    • So, a holds the address of the array arr[1].

    • *a effectively gives us the array arr[1] (which decays to a pointer to arr[1][0]).

  2. Evaluating the Target &arr[1][2]:

    • This is the address of the element at index 2 of the second row.

  3. Evaluating the Options:

    • A. &a[0][2]: a[0] is *(a+0) which is *a (the array arr[1]). a[0][2] accesses the element at index 2. & takes the address. This is valid and correct.

    • B. (*a+2): *a is the array arr[1]. In an expression, it decays to a pointer to the first integer (&arr[1][0]). Adding 2 (+2) moves the pointer forward by 2 integers. This results in the address of arr[1][2]. This is also valid and correct.

    • C. (int *)(&arr+1)-1: &arr+1 points to the memory immediately after the entire 2D array. Casting to int* and subtracting 1 moves back one integer, which is the last element of the array (arr[1][2]). This is also numerically correct.

    • D. *(a+2): This would point to a row 2 steps ahead of a, which is out of bounds.

Now, $\texttt{\&arr[1][2]}$ means the address of the last element of the array.

    Correct. $\texttt{*a}$ refers to the row $\texttt{arr[1]}$.
    So $\texttt{*a+2}$ points to the third element of that row, which is $\texttt{\&arr[1][2]}$.
  • C. $\texttt{(int\ *)\ (\&arr+1)-1}$
    Correct. $\texttt{\&arr+1}$ points just after the whole 2D array.
    After casting it to $\texttt{int\ *}$ and subtracting $1$, it points to the last integer element of the array.

    Incorrect. Since $\texttt{a}$ already points to $\texttt{arr[1]}$, $\texttt{a+2}$ moves beyond the valid rows of the array. So this is not the same as $\texttt{\&arr[1][2]}$.

And $\texttt{arrop[2]}$ points to $\texttt{twoD[0][0]}$, whose value is $1$.

So,

$\boxed{\texttt{*pp[1]=1}}$

(*c)[1] we can write as *((*c) + 1), first c is pointing to the 1st row, de-referencing it will give integer pointer pointing to the 0th index of 1st row, (*c) + 1 will point to the 1st index of 1st row and *((*c) + 1) will give value and we are changing it to 6.

So after the operations array will change to

So a[2][0] = 5 and a[1][0] = 10

  • c now points to a[1] — i.e., {10,20}.

In the function parameter,

$\texttt{int\ c[2][2]}$

is treated as:

$\texttt{int\ (*c)[2]}$

So $\texttt{c}$ is actually a pointer to an array of $2$ integers. Therefore, this statement is valid:

$\texttt{c\ =\ c+1;}$

Initially, $\texttt{c}$ points to $\texttt{a[0]}$.

After $\texttt{c\ =\ c+1;}$, $\texttt{c}$ points to $\texttt{a[1]}$.

Now,

$\texttt{*c[1]\ =\ 5;}$

means:

$\texttt{*(c[1])\ =\ 5;}$

Since $\texttt{c}$ is pointing to $\texttt{a[1]}$, $\texttt{c[1]}$ refers to $\texttt{a[2]}$.

So $\texttt{*c[1]\ =\ 5;}$ changes $\texttt{a[2][0]}$ to $5$.

Next,

$\texttt{(*c)[1]\ =\ 6;}$

Since $\texttt{c}$ points to $\texttt{a[1]}$, this changes $\texttt{a[1][1]}$ to $6$.

Finally,

$\texttt{printf("\%d\ \%d",\ a[2][0],\ a[1][0]);}$

prints $\texttt{a[2][0]}$ and $\texttt{a[1][0]}$.

Here, $\texttt{a[2][0]=5}$ and $\texttt{a[1][0]=10}$.

Final output: $\texttt{5\ 10}$

Correct option: A.
